payload.decision: Rank authors by distinct 2021–2024 snapshot works with a Columbia-system affiliation on that author’s own byline, including snapshot child institutions and all work types; break publication-count ties by OpenAlex author ID. Assign one field–subfield to each researcher using the most frequent field and then the most frequent subfield within that field, based on primary OpenAlex topics on their Columbia-affiliated works (deterministic ID tie-breaks). A collaboration edge counts distinct snapshot works shared by two of the selected researchers regardless of the affiliations on that particular work.

payload.brief:
USER QUESTION: Show the collaboration network among Columbia's 80 most prolific researchers in 2021-2024 with hierarchical edge bundling, grouping the researchers by field and subfield so that cross-field collaborations stand out.
GOAL: Build ranking, topic group assignments and coauthorship inputs.
INPUTS: none
DEFINITIONS: Rank authors by distinct 2021–2024 snapshot works with a Columbia-system affiliation on that author’s own byline, including snapshot child institutions and all work types; break publication-count ties by OpenAlex author ID. Assign one field–subfield to each researcher using the most frequent field and then the most frequent subfield within that field, based on primary OpenAlex topics on their Columbia-affiliated works (deterministic ID tie-breaks); missing topic works do not vote. A collaboration edge counts distinct snapshot works shared by two of the selected researchers regardless of the affiliations on that particular work.
ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA: Exactly 80 unique authors with stable ID, display name, rank, publication count, field/subfield IDs and labels (unknown if no topic), and topic coverage/strength if feasible. Confirm true primary topic handling and exact Columbia institution IDs used. Supply deduped work-author incidences restricted to these 80 for all snapshot coauthorships, or aggregated unique pair edges with shared-work counts as preferred. Keep isolates in nodes. Characterize ties/caveats.
OUTPUT: Save analysis-ready artifacts, report IDs, schemas and validation, and any material caveats.

payload.result:
Dataset: Columbia University publications, 2021-2024 (OpenAlex snapshot of 2026-11-23)
Works (papers, preprints, books, datasets, ...) published 2021-2024 with at least one author affiliated with Columbia University (OpenAlex institution I78577930 and its OpenAlex child institutions: NASA GISS, Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory, ICAP, CZ Biohub NY), taken from the OpenAlex API on 2026-11-23 and never refreshed. Includes all co-authors and their institutions, the OpenAlex topic hierarchy, profiles of Columbia-affiliated authors, venues, outgoing references, yearly citation counts, keywords and funders.

Tables:
- authors (29,518 rows): Profiles of authors who are Columbia-affiliated on at least one snapshot work.
- authorship_institutions (619,528 rows): Institutions listed by each author on each work (an author can list se

- citations lists every outgoing reference; only rows with cited_in_snapshot = true point to works that are themselves in this dataset (and therefore have metadata here).
- authors contains profiles only for authors who are Columbia-affiliated on at least one work in the snapshot; other co-authors appear only in authorships (name and id).
- Profile metrics in authors and sources (works_count, cited_by_count, h_index, ...) are global OpenAlex values for the whole career / whole venue, not restricted to this snapshot.
- Some works have no abstract (abstract is NULL), no topic, or no source.

Counting rules:
- authorships has one row per (work, author); count works with count(DISTINCT work_id) after joining it.
- authorships.is_columbia is true when that author lists a Columbia institution on that specific work.
- A work can have up to 3 topics in work_topics; works.primary_topic_* gives the single primary one.
- work_topics joins to topics for the full hierarchy domain > field > subfield > topic.

- works.work_id = authorships.work_id

payload.decision: Use 2021–2024 snapshot works of all types. A resolved OpenAlex author qualifies for an individual work only when their own (work_id, author_order) has one or more of I78577930, I152304114, I116578957, I4387154024, I4396570641; this exactly matches the snapshot authorship is_columbia flag. Deduplicate (author_id, work_id) before ranking, order by distinct work count descending then literal OpenAlex author ID ascending, and use author profile names (validate coverage).

Each distinct qualifying author–work pair votes using works.primary_topic_id joined to topics; no alternate topics or score ranking. Select plurality field, then plurality subfield conditional on the winning field, breaking ties by ascending numeric hierarchy ID. Missing primary hierarchy abstains; if no votes, use null IDs and Unknown labels. Coverage = voting works / qualifying works; field strength = winning field votes / voting works; subfield strength = winning subfield votes / winning field votes. Emit count of tied winners for both levels.

Use the full snapshot bylines, with no Columbia filter on either endpoint, for coauthorship among the selected 80. Deduplicate (work_id, author_id), then emit one undirected pair (lexically smaller author ID first) weighted by distinct shared work IDs; retain all selected authors in nodes even if they have no edges. Cross-field means both assigned field IDs are known and differ.

base = '''WITH qualifying AS (
 SELECT DISTINCT a.author_id, a.work_id
 FROM authorships a JOIN works w USING (work_id)
 WHERE a.author_id IS NOT NULL AND w.publication_year BETWEEN 2021 AND 2024
   AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM authorship_institutions i
     WHERE i.work_id=a.work_id AND i.author_order=a.author_order
       AND i.institution_id IN ('I78577930','I152304114','I116578957','I4387154024','I4396570641'))
), counts AS (
 SELECT author_id,count(*) AS publication_count FROM qualifying GROUP BY author_id
), ranked AS (
 SELECT *, row_number() OVER (ORDER BY publication_count DESC, author_id ASC) AS rank,
 count(*) OVER (PARTITION BY publication_count) AS publication_count_tie_size FROM counts
), selected AS (SELECT * FROM ranked WHERE rank<=80)'''
print(sql(base+''' SELECT count(*) candidates, sum(publication_count) incidences, max(publication_count) max_works, count(*) filter(where p.author_id is null) missing_profiles, count(*) filter(where publication_count<>p.works_in_snapshot) profile_counts_differ FROM ranked r LEFT JOIN authors p USING(author_id)''').to_string(index=False))
print(sql(base+''' SELECT rank,author_id,name,publication_count,publication_count_tie_size FROM ranked JOIN authors USING(author_id) WHERE rank<=3 OR rank BETWEEN 75 AND 85 ORDER BY rank''').to_string(index=False))
print(sql('SELECT count(distinct type) AS work_types, max(authors_count) AS max_authors, count(*) AS works FROM works').to_string(index=False))

STATUS: done

ARTIFACTS:  
T1 - Columbia top 80 researchers — ranked hierarchy nodes - one row per selected OpenAlex author, including isolates - 80 rows  
T2 - Columbia top 80 researchers — weighted coauthorship edges - one row per unordered author pair with at least one shared snapshot work - 208 rows

**Schemas**
- **T1:** `author_id`, `display_name`, `rank`, `publication_count`, `publication_count_tie_size`, `field_id`, `field`, `subfield_id`, `subfield`, `topic_works`, `topic_coverage`, `field_votes`, `field_strength`, `field_tie_size`, `subfield_votes`, `subfield_strength`, `subfield_tie_size`.
- **T2:** `source_author_id`, `target_author_id`, `shared_work_count`, `cross_field`. Edges are undirected; the smaller author ID is stored first.

**DEFINITIONS**
- **Ranking:** Counted distinct 2021–2024 snapshot works of all 24 work types only when the author’s own byline listed a qualifying institution. Ranked by count descending, then OpenAlex author ID ascending. The five institution IDs exactly reproduced the snapshot’s byline-level Columbia flag: Columbia University (`I78577930`), Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory (`I152304114`), Goddard Institute for Space Studies (`I116578957`), ICAP Global Health (`I4387154024`), and Chan Zuckerberg Biohub New York (`I4396570641`).
- **Hierarchy:** Used the true primary topic, `works.primary_topic_id`, joined to `topics`. No secondary topics or topic scores were used. Each qualifying work with a primary topic cast one vote. The most frequent field won, then the most frequent subfield **within that field**; ties went to the lower numeric ID. Coverage is the share of qualifying works that voted. Field strength is the winning field’s share of those votes; subfield strength is the winning subfield’s share of votes within that field.
- **Edges:** Counted distinct shared snapshot works after deduplicating work–author pairs, regardless of whether either selected author listed Columbia on that work. `cross_field` compares the researchers’ assigned fields, not the shared work’s topic.

**VALIDATION**
- Exactly **80 unique authors** with nonmissing display names and ranks 1–80. Four authors tied at **71 works** for ranks 79–82. The ID rule placed Jeffrey L. Shaman and David R. Reichman inside the cutoff.
- The authors span **14 fields and 35 subfields**. Primary topics were available for **8,173 of 8,191** qualifying author–work pairs; every nonmissing primary topic ID matched the hierarchy. All 80 authors received assignments. One field tie was resolved by ID; there were no winning-subfield ties.
- **208 unique edges**, including **94 cross-field edges**. The edge weights sum to **1,781 pair–work incidences** across **1,054 distinct shared works**. **15 isolates** remain in T1.

**CAVEATS**  
The network covers only the frozen OpenAlex snapshot, not the researchers’ complete collaboration histories. Works with more than 100 authors are excluded. Columbia University Irving Medical Center, Barnard College, and Teachers College do not qualify on their own. Unresolved author IDs cannot be ranked or linked, and OpenAlex author disambiguation and topic classification may contain errors. The assigned field is a plurality of an author’s qualifying works, not necessarily a majority or a formal departmental affiliation.

**NOTES FOR NEXT STEP**  
Build the bundling hierarchy as `root → field_id → subfield_id → author_id`, using T1 for every leaf so isolates remain visible. Join T2 by author ID, use `shared_work_count` for edge weight, and highlight `cross_field` edges. Medicine contains 44 of the 80 authors, so the hierarchy is uneven.

payload.text:
STATUS: done

## FINDINGS

**Cross-field collaborations accounted for 45.2% of author ties but only 23.4% of the total collaboration weight.** Among Columbia’s top 80 researchers in the 2021–2024 snapshot, 94 of 208 observed coauthor pairs crossed assigned fields. Those pairs accounted for 417 of 1,781 pair–work incidences; the 114 within-field ties accounted for the other 1,364. The hierarchy contained 14 fields and 35 subfields, and 15 researchers had no ties to others in the top 80. [F1]

| Field pair | Author ties | Pair–work incidences |
|---|---:|---:|
| Environmental Science × Medicine | **21 (1st)** | 39 |
| Biochemistry, Genetics and Molecular Biology × Medicine | 16 (2nd) | **73 (1st)** |
| Medicine × Social Sciences | 11 (3rd) | 34 |
| Engineering × Physics and Astronomy | 4 | 69 (2nd) |
| Materials Science × Physics and Astronomy | 4 | 54 (3rd) |

The top three ranks were untied for each metric. Environmental Science × Medicine connected the most distinct author pairs, while Biochemistry, Genetics and Molecular Biology × Medicine had the highest summed weight. [F2]

The **unique strongest cross-field author tie** was **Michal F. Lipson** (Engineering) and **Alexander L. Gaeta** (Physics and Astronomy), with **57 shared works**. That one tie accounted for **82.6%** of the Engineering × Physics and Astronomy bundle’s weight. [F3]

## ARTIFACTS

- `T3` - Collaboration totals by field status - 3-row table of counts and shares.
- `T4` - Cross-field collaboration by field pair - 18-row table with field IDs, roster sizes, counts, and ranks.
- `T5` - Strongest cross-field author ties - 1-row table with author IDs, hierarchy labels, and shared-work count.

## METHOD

Used T1’s publication-ranked roster and plurality primary-topic field and subfield assignments. Validated that T2 contained unique unordered pairs with positive integer weights, that all endpoints were on the roster, and that the cross-field flags matched T1. Aggregated by unordered field pair and ranked separately by tie count and summed weight. T1 and T2 remain the inputs for the separate bundled visualization.

## CAVEATS

These are raw counts. Medicine had 44 of the 80 researchers, compared with 9 in Environmental Science and 3 in Biochemistry, Genetics and Molecular Biology, so the field pairs had different numbers of possible ties. [F2] The rankings do not measure a field’s propensity to collaborate. Summed weights count **pair–work incidences**, not distinct publications across the network: one work can contribute to several author pairs.

**WHAT IT SHOWS:** A circular, hierarchically bundled network of Columbia’s 80 most prolific researchers in 2021–2024. Purple emphasizes the **94 cross-field collaborations** out of 208; same-field links are muted. Outer bands identify 14 fields, inner segments identify 35 subfields, and hollow dots mark the 15 researchers with no links in this network. Thicker curves represent more shared works. Curves follow the grouping hierarchy, not intermediary researchers.

Search by name, field, subfield, or stable author ID. Hover over a researcher for their exact rank, publication count, field, and subfield; select them to see their collaborators and shared-work counts. Hover over a link for its exact weight. The host highlight entity type for researchers is `author`.

**PARAMETERS**
- `edge_scope` — Show all collaborations (default) or cross-field collaborations only.
- `min_shared_works` — Show links with at least this many shared works, from 1 to 85 (default 1).

Both filters change only the links; all researchers and groupings stay in place.

**BROWSER QA:** The default and selected browser renders were reviewed. Automated checks passed for hover, click selection, visible highlighting, multi-item state, and both parameter updates. The independent gate approved `V1`.

**LIMITATIONS:** Several upper-left field labels are tightly spaced, and individual curves can be hard to trace in dense bundles. Use the researcher’s collaborator list for exact pairwise counts. Automated QA did not independently assert routing control points, detail values against the source tables, or node preservation after filtering.

payload.text:
**94 of the 208 coauthor ties (45.2%) crossed fields** among Columbia’s 80 most prolific researchers in the 2021–2024 OpenAlex snapshot. Cross-field ties accounted for 417 of 1,781 pair–work counts (23.4%). A work with several researchers can count toward several pairs. [T3]

In the interactive network, **purple curves connect researchers in different fields**, muted curves connect researchers in the same field, and thicker curves mean more shared works. The outer ring groups researchers by field and subfield. Curves bundle along that hierarchy; they don’t imply collaboration through an intermediary. Search or select a researcher to see their collaborators and exact shared-work counts. Switch to **cross-field only** or raise the **minimum shared works** to reduce clutter without moving or hiding researchers. [V1]

- **Environmental Science ↔ Medicine** connected the most distinct cross-field author pairs: **21**. [T4]
- **Biochemistry, Genetics and Molecular Biology ↔ Medicine** had the highest summed cross-field weight: **73 pair–work counts**. These are raw totals, not adjusted for field size. [T4]
- **Michal F. Lipson (Engineering) ↔ Alexander L. Gaeta (Physics and Astronomy)** was the strongest individual cross-field tie, with **57 shared works**. [T5]

Researchers were ranked by distinct snapshot works listing Columbia or an included affiliate on their own byline. Fields and subfields reflect the most frequent primary OpenAlex topics on those works, not departmental appointments. The network uses only shared works in the snapshot, so it does not capture researchers’ full collaboration histories. [T1, T2]

Two follow-ups: Which researchers connect to the widest range of fields? Which field pairs stand out after accounting for the number of possible author pairs?
